questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

fix(install): an instruction file with an archy begin marker but no end marker loses every user line after the marker on install, and is deleted outright on uninstall
## Problem

`_marker_block_range` (`src/archy/install/base.py:122-140`) treats EOF as the end of the archy block when `<!-- archy:end -->` is missing. That recovery is deliberate (#336 pins it) and is right for the shape #336 had in mind, a file truncated inside the block. But if the user deleted the end marker (or a merge dropped it) and then wrote their own notes below, everything from the begin marker to EOF is treated as archy's:

- `archy install` replaces it with a fresh block: every user line after the marker is gone, with no prompt and no note;
- `archy uninstall` removes it; if nothing non-whitespace precedes the marker, `remove_instructions` returns `None` and the whole file is unlinked.

This contradicts `upsert_instructions`' docstring (`base.py:143-148`: "Other content in the file (the user's own CLAUDE.md, an existing AGENTS.md) is preserved") and `docs/INSTALL.md:45-46` ("unrelated config in shared files is preserved"). The files involved are the user's global `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` / `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`.

## Reproduction

Under a throwaway `HOME`:

```bash
B=$(mktemp -d)/repro-marker && mkdir -p "$B/a/home/.claude" "$B/b/home/.claude" "$B/proj" && cd "$B/proj"

# install: user notes after a begin marker with no end marker
printf '# My global rules\n- rule A\n\n<!-- archy:begin -->\nold archy text\n\n## My own section after\n- important user note\n' > "$B/a/home/.claude/CLAUDE.md"
env HOME="$B/a/home" archy install --target claude -y | head -1
grep -c 'important user note' "$B/a/home/.claude/CLAUDE.md"

# uninstall: marker at the top of the file
printf '<!-- archy:begin -->\nold archy text\n\n## My notes\n- precious 1\n' > "$B/b/home/.claude/CLAUDE.md"
env HOME="$B/b/home" archy uninstall --target claude -y | head -1
ls "$B/b/home/.claude/CLAUDE.md"
```

Actual:

```
Wrote 3 file(s):
0
Cleaned up 1 file(s):
ls: .../b/home/.claude/CLAUDE.md: No such file or directory
```

## Expected

archy wrote only what lies between its two markers. With no end marker, archy cannot know where its text stops, so it must not guess in the destructive direction: `## My own section after` / `- important user note` and `## My notes` / `- precious 1` survive, and the user is told the block is malformed.

## Suggested fix

When the begin marker exists and the end marker does not, refuse with an `InstallError` naming the file and the line of the begin marker ("archy:begin at line N has no matching archy:end; delete the stray line or add the end marker, then re-run"), for both install and uninstall. Surface the same in `--print-config` / `--dry-run`. Update #336's test, which pins the recovery, to pin the refusal instead (or keep EOF recovery only when nothing follows the marker but archy's own known block text).

## Test

- Fixture shapes that reach the branch: (a) user text before AND after a begin marker with no end marker; (b) begin marker on line 1, user text after, no end marker. Assert first that the fixture contains `INSTRUCTIONS_BEGIN` and not `INSTRUCTIONS_END`.
- For install and uninstall on each: assert the user lines are byte-identical afterwards (and the file still exists), and that an error naming the file is raised or printed.
- Mutation check: restore EOF recovery, confirm red.

## Notes

- Related: #336 (closed; pins the truncated-block recovery), #278 (closed; the shared locator), #697 (open; uninstall can delete a shared config and the tests stay green).
- Severity: low by trigger frequency (the end marker has to be deleted first), but the effect is silent loss of user-authored text, including whole-file deletion on uninstall; weigh up if data loss is the priority.
- Found by the 2026-11-04 codebase audit, verified by an independent reproduction. Cited lines are on `main` at ee431ef.

fix(install): an instruction file with an archy begin marker but no end marker loses every user line after the marker on install, and is deleted outright on uninstall
## Problem

`_marker_block_range` (`src/archy/install/base.py:122-140`) treats EOF as the end of the archy block when `<!-- archy:end -->` is missing. That recovery is deliberate (#336 pins it) and is right for the shape #336 had in mind, a file truncated inside the block. But if the user deleted the end marker (or a merge dropped it) and then wrote their own notes below, everything from the begin marker to EOF is treated as archy's:

- `archy install` replaces it with a fresh block: every user line after the marker is gone, with no prompt and no note;
- `archy uninstall` removes it; if nothing non-whitespace precedes the marker, `remove_instructions` returns `None` and the whole file is unlinked.

This contradicts `upsert_instructions`' docstring (`base.py:143-148`: "Other content in the file (the user's own CLAUDE.md, an existing AGENTS.md) is preserved") and `docs/INSTALL.md:45-46` ("unrelated config in shared files is preserved"). The files involved are the user's global `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` / `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`.

## Reproduction

Under a throwaway `HOME`:

```bash
B=$(mktemp -d)/repro-marker && mkdir -p "$B/a/home/.claude" "$B/b/home/.claude" "$B/proj" && cd "$B/proj"

# install: user notes after a begin marker with no end marker
printf '# My global rules\n- rule A\n\n<!-- archy:begin -->\nold archy text\n\n## My own section after\n- important user note\n' > "$B/a/home/.claude/CLAUDE.md"
env HOME="$B/a/home" archy install --target claude -y | head -1
grep -c 'important user note' "$B/a/home/.claude/CLAUDE.md"

# uninstall: marker at the top of the file
printf '<!-- archy:begin -->\nold archy text\n\n## My notes\n- precious 1\n' > "$B/b/home/.claude/CLAUDE.md"
env HOME="$B/b/home" archy uninstall --target claude -y | head -1
ls "$B/b/home/.claude/CLAUDE.md"
```

Actual:

```
Wrote 3 file(s):
0
Cleaned up 1 file(s):
ls: .../b/home/.claude/CLAUDE.md: No such file or directory
```

## Expected

archy wrote only what lies between its two markers. With no end marker, archy cannot know where its text stops, so it must not guess in the destructive direction: `## My own section after` / `- important user note` and `## My notes` / `- precious 1` survive, and the user is told the block is malformed.

## Suggested fix

When the begin marker exists and the end marker does not, refuse with an `InstallError` naming the file and the line of the begin marker ("archy:begin at line N has no matching archy:end; delete the stray line or add the end marker, then re-run"), for both install and uninstall. Surface the same in `--print-config` / `--dry-run`. Update #336's test, which pins the recovery, to pin the refusal instead (or keep EOF recovery only when nothing follows the marker but archy's own known block text).

## Test

- Fixture shapes that reach the branch: (a) user text before AND after a begin marker with no end marker; (b) begin marker on line 1, user text after, no end marker. Assert first that the fixture contains `INSTRUCTIONS_BEGIN` and not `INSTRUCTIONS_END`.
- For install and uninstall on each: assert the user lines are byte-identical afterwards (and the file still exists), and that an error naming the file is raised or printed.
- Mutation check: restore EOF recovery, confirm red.

## Notes

- Related: #336 (closed; pins the truncated-block recovery), #278 (closed; the shared locator), #697 (open; uninstall can delete a shared config and the tests stay green).
- Severity: low by trigger frequency (the end marker has to be deleted first), but the effect is silent loss of user-authored text, including whole-file deletion on uninstall; weigh up if data loss is the priority.
- Found by the 2026-11-04 codebase audit, verified by an independent reproduction. Cited lines are on `main` at ee431ef.

def _without_archy(action: FileAction, rendered: str) -> str:
    """``unrender(rendered)``, or for a file archy owns, its non-archy text.

    An owned file's unrender deletes it (``None``). If install keeps user text
    outside a marker block (``upsert_instructions``), that text is the baseline,
    so it never prints; a file with no markers is archy's whole (``""``).

    stripped = action.unrender(rendered)
    if stripped is not None:

    kept = remove_instructions(rendered)
    return "" if kept is None or kept == rendered else kept


def preview_config(
    adapter_id: str,
    scope: Scope,
    *,
    project_root: Path | None = None,
    seed_permissions: bool = True,
) -> list[ConfigPreview]:

    ws = DryRunWriteSystem()

    previews: list[ConfigPreview] = []
    for action in plan:
        existing_text = ws.read_text(action.path)
        try:

            raise

        existing = action.path.read_bytes().decode("utf-8") if action.path.exists() else None
        previews.append(

content.content:
decide: which re-export target is right when a re-exported name is itself a module?
open
Split out of #419, which shared two of the three import-resolution algorithms between `graph` and `conventions`. This is the third, and it is **a decision rather than a refactor**, which is why it was not folded in: #419 required behaviour preservation on both sides, and unifying these changes one of them.

## The divergence

For `from .x import y` inside a package `__init__.py`, **where `pkg.x.y` is itself a module**:

| side | maps `y` to | code |
|---|---|---|
| `conventions._reexport_maps` | `pkg.x.y` | `source = f"{base}.{name}" if f"{base}.{name}" in known else base` |
| `graph._build_reexport_maps` | `pkg.x` | `_reexport_source` returns the from-module |

A consumer writing `from pkg import y` then resolves to `pkg.x.y` through the lookup and to `pkg.x` through the graph.

The two agree in every other case, and #419's cross-check found **zero disagreements across all 44 `archy.*` modules**, so this shape does not currently occur in archy's own source. It is latent, not live.

## Which is right

`conventions` looks more precise: if `pkg.x.y` is a module, `from pkg import y` really does reach that module, and stopping at `pkg.x` under-reports. But "more precise" is the claim to check, not to assume:

- Does `from .x import y` in an `__init__.py` where `x.y` is a module actually re-export the MODULE, or can it re-export a symbol named `y` that shadows it? Both are legal; the shadowing case makes `pkg.x` the correct answer and `pkg.x.y` wrong.
- Changing `graph` changes the **dependency graph**, and therefore `check`, `cycles`, `score` and every bench number derived from them. That is not a silent change.
- Changing `conventions` instead makes the lookup less precise to match, which is the wrong direction if `conventions` is right.

## What this needs

1. A tree exercising the shape, in both the module-shadowed and symbol-shadowed forms.
2. A decision on which answer is correct for each, written down before either side is edited.
3. If `graph` changes: check whether any bench baseline or `docs/CASE_STUDIES.md` number moves, since a changed edge set can move the score.

Until then the two implementations stay separate **on purpose**, and both carry a comment saying so. That is worse than one implementation and better than a unification that silently picks a winner.

## Constraints

- Whichever side changes, `conventions --module` and `archy impact` must still agree on archy's own source. #419 added `test_lookup_resolves_the_five_shapes_that_used_to_disagree`, which pins the answers; extend it rather than asserting mere agreement, which is tautological now that the core resolver is shared.

def test_lookup_resolves_each_import_shape_to_a_distinct_module(tmp_path: Path):
    """Pin the ANSWERS, and make each shape reach somewhere only it can reach.

    Two earlier drafts of this test looked stronger than they were, so the
    fixture is built against both failures.

    The first asserted only that the lookup and the graph AGREE, which is
    tautological now that both call `graph.resolve_from_import`: break the
    shared function and both break identically, so they still agree.

    The second pinned answers but let the submodule shape and the relative
    shape resolve to the SAME module, so the set collapsed them and an
    off-by-one in `resolve_relative_import`'s level arithmetic still passed.
    Every shape below therefore resolves somewhere no other shape reaches.
    """
    pkg = tmp_path / "app"
    (pkg / "sub").mkdir(parents=True)
    (pkg / "__init__.py").write_text("from app.impl import Thing\n")
    (pkg / "impl.py").write_text("Thing = 1\n")
    (pkg / "sibling.py").write_text("x = 1\n")
    # Reachable ONLY through the two-level relative walk below, so nothing else
    # in this fixture can put it in the result set.
    (pkg / "only_via_relative.py").write_text("y = 1\n")
    (pkg / "sub" / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (pkg / "sub" / "uses.py").write_text(
        "from app import Thing\n"  # a re-exported name routes to the DEFINING module
        "from app import sibling\n"  # a submodule is an edge to the submodule
        "from .. import only_via_relative\n"  # walks up out of the subpackage
    )

    resolved = set(compute_module_view(tmp_path, "app.sub.uses").imports_internal)

    # `from app import Thing` must not stop at the package: `app.impl` defines it.
    assert "app.impl" in resolved
    # `from app import sibling` is the submodule, never the bare package.
    assert "app.sibling" in resolved
    # Only the `..` walk can reach this one, so it fails if level handling breaks.
    assert "app.only_via_relative" in resolved
    # Attributing the submodule import to `app` as well was one of the five.
    assert "app" not in resolved

    # And the graph, the surface the lookup must never contradict, agrees.
    g = build_graph(tmp_path)
    internal = {n for n, d in g.nodes(data=True) if not d.get("external")}
    assert {t for t in g.successors("app.sub.uses") if t in internal} == resolved

cat > /tmp/b436.md <<'E'
Closes #436.

**Decision:** `conventions` now stops at the re-exporting submodule (`pkg.x`), matching `graph`. No graph, `check`, `cycles` or score change, since only the `conventions` lookup moved.

**Why `pkg.x`.** I ran both shapes under real Python. With `from .x import y` in `pkg/__init__.py` and `x/y.py` present:
- `x` defines no `y`: `pkg.y` is the module `pkg.x.y`.
- `x` defines a symbol `y`: `pkg.y` is the symbol, and `y.py` is never imported (attribute wins over submodule).

The syntax cannot tell these apart, and `pkg.x` is a true edge in both. Before, `conventions --module` reported `pkg.x.y` for the second shape, an import the program never makes. Telling them apart would need a top-level-bindings fact in the parser, and star imports defeat even that.

**Bench (brief).** Scanned the 28 manifest projects (shallow clones of default branch, not pinned SHAs) for this shape: 11 sites, in numpy, pytorch, setuptools (vendored) and sqlalchemy (3 hits there are macOS case-insensitive false positives). numpy's `_core.memmap` is a real case where a simple "x does not bind y" guess is wrong, because `memmap` arrives through a star import. Rare, but both shapes occur, and a guess for the module shape is wrong for real code.

**Known under-report.** In the module shape, a consumer's `from pkg import y` now resolves to `pkg.x`, not `pkg.x.y`. The `pkg -> pkg.x.y` edge in `graph` for the package itself is unchanged and still over-reports in the symbol shape; left alone since it changes the graph.

**Tests.** `test_lookup_stops_at_the_reexporting_submodule_when_the_name_is_also_a_module` covers both shapes and asserts the answer (`{"app.x"}`) on both the lookup and the graph. Both cases fail with the old line restored.

Gates: ruff check/format, ty, pytest (1824 passed), `archy check`, `cycles --strict`, headers, contracts.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

content.text:
PR #828 is open at https://github.com/hslee16/Archy/pull/828 and closes #436. The `conventions` lookup now stops at `pkg.x`, matching `graph`. I haven't run a DeepWork review round on it yet.

**Bench.** I scanned shallow clones of the 28 manifest projects, taken from each default branch rather than the pinned SHAs.
- **How often the shape occurs:** there were 11 sites, so it is rare.
- **Where:** numpy, pytorch and vendored setuptools had the module shape. sqlalchemy's 3 hits are false positives from macOS's case-insensitive filesystem.
- **numpy's `_core.memmap`:** this is a real case where guessing "module" would be wrong. It looks like a module, but the name comes from a star import, so it is probably the class. A parser fact about top-level names would not catch it either.

**Why `pkg.x`**
- **Real Python behaviour:** I ran both shapes. If `x` defines a symbol `y`, that symbol wins and `y.py` is never imported. If it doesn't, `pkg.y` is the module `pkg.x.y`.
- **What the syntax can tell:** `pkg.x` is a real edge in both cases, and the syntax can't tell the two shapes apart.
- **What the old code got wrong:** `conventions --module` claimed `pkg.x.y` in both shapes, which is a false import in the symbol shape.

**Verification**
- **Tests:** the new test covers both shapes and asserts `{"app.x"}` from both the lookup and the graph. Both cases fail when I put the old line back.
- **Gates:** pytest (1824 passed), ruff, ty, `archy check`, `cycles --strict`, headers and contracts all pass.
- **Score:** `graph` is untouched, so no score or bench number moves.

**Known limit.** In the module shape, a consumer's `from pkg import y` now resolves to `pkg.x`, not `pkg.x.y`. That under-reports slightly. The graph's own `pkg -> pkg.x.y` edge is still a false edge in the symbol shape. I left it because fixing it would change graph edges. I can file it as a follow-up if you want.

Do you want me to run a DeepWork review round on #828 before you look at it?

content.content:
decide: should the graph name its own blind spots (opaque dynamic-import sites), and does the count change an agent decision?
open
## The question

Should archy detect and report *opaque* dynamic-import sites - `importlib.import_module(...)`, `__import__(...)`, entry-point loading, string-keyed factories - as an explicit blind-spot list, rather than silently omitting the edges it cannot resolve?

Not resolving them. Naming them. "This package contains 3 sites where an import target is computed at runtime; the graph below does not include whatever they load."

## Where this comes from

`docs/FUTURE.md:81` already anticipated it and deferred it:

> **Dynamic imports** - `importlib.import_module(name)` where `name` is a runtime string. Static analysis can flag these as opaque but can't resolve them. Acceptable.

The prompt to revisit is Stéphane Derosiaux, ["Frontier AI: Claude Code and Codex Still Use grep. Why?"](https://levelup.gitconnected.com/claude-code-and-codex-still-search-code-like-its-1975-that-s-not-an-accident-8f70cb9897ea) (Sep 2026), on the model boundary of structured tools: a call graph looks *complete* where `Class.forName(config.get("processor"))` is doing the wiring, and the text is what reveals the real link. An under-approximation that does not advertise its own edges is the failure mode being described.

The parser already walks every `(call)` node (`src/archy/parser.py`, `_CALL_QUERY`), so the detection site exists; this would be a new `CallRef`-adjacent capture plus a count carried through the graph, not new machinery.

## Why this is a `decide:` and not a `feat:`

Nobody has asked for it. Measured usage is under 20 real users, and the standing rule here is that features get weighed against the usage signal before being built. Same gate as #427.

It also has to pass the anti-theater test, which the docs-only sibling tickets (#474, #475) pass trivially and this one does not automatically: **does the number change what the agent does?** The case for yes: `impacted: []` plus "and there are 3 opaque import sites in this package" is a different decision from `impacted: []` alone. The case for no: an agent that has read #474's caveat already knows to grep before deleting, and a raw count with no target adds a number without adding an action.

The distinguishing test, and what should be settled before any code: is there a real repository where the dynamic-import count is *low enough to be actionable* (a handful of sites you can actually go read) rather than either zero or a wall of framework noise? If every repo shows either 0 or 200, the signal is not one.

## Open sub-questions

- What counts? `importlib.import_module` and `__import__` are unambiguous. Entry points, `__getattr__` module hooks and string-keyed registries each need their own argument.
- Where does it surface? A count on `archy_graph`, or scoped to the query in `archy_impact` (only sites inside the impacted set), which is the version more likely to change a decision.
- Does a constant-string `importlib.import_module("a.b.c")` become a real edge? That is resolvable and arguably a bug in the graph today rather than a blind spot to report.

## Done when

Either a written decision to close this as declined with the reason recorded, or a scoping pass that answers the distinguishing test above with data from real repositories - before any implementation.

hslee16: Data for sub-question 3 ("does a constant-string `importlib.import_module("a.b.c")` become a real edge?"), widened to string literals generally (`mock.patch("pkg.mod.fn")`, `monkeypatch.setattr("...")`, settings and task paths). Posted here as input to this decision, not as a new ticket.

**Prior art.** Two tools ship this as an opt-in heuristic. Pants `[python-infer]` has `string_imports` (default false), `string_imports_min_dots` (default 2), a `string_import_ignore` glob list and a `# pants: no-infer-dep` pragma. Ruff `[analyze]` has `detect-string-imports` (default false) and `string-imports-min-dots` (default 2), and ruff PR #24058 added a shorter-prefix fallback, so `"pkg.mod.fn"` resolves to `pkg.mod`. These are config docs, not precision data.

**Measured 2026-10-23.** `ruff analyze graph` with and without `--detect-string-imports` (ruff 0.15.12, min-dots 2) over the 40 `bench/cache/contract_clones` repos:
- 24 of 40 repos gain edges; 1,281 new edges in total.
- 938 of them come from test files.
- 593 test-sourced edges reach a module the test does not already reach statically. Those are tests `affected` misses today, spread over about 19 to 20 repos.
- Spot checks among those are true dependencies for test selection: `patch("thegent.agents.teammate_runner.TeammateRunner")`, `importlib.import_module("docvet.checks.freshness")` in a test, `monkeypatch.setattr("aai_cli.commands.llm.gateway.complete")`.
- Known false positives for architecture: logger names such as `LoggerAdapter("pkg.domain.abnormal")`.
- Fan-out risk: string edges into hub modules can make `affected` select nearly everything. 15M4C4R/ecosistemas-flujos-ia gains 85,848 (test, module) reachability pairs and AviralGup7/Singularity-Zero 17,869. The depth cap of 5 limits this only partly.
- The originally proposed example (mcp_coder) is not one: all 31 of its string edges are already reachable statically.

**How this bears on the distinguishing test.** The issue asks whether there is a repo where the signal is actionable rather than 0 or a wall of noise. For literal strings in tests, the answer looks like yes in about half the corpus. But the fan-out outliers show the noise case exists too.

**Where two independent reviewers split.**
- One reads it as a correctness fix to `affected`: over-selecting tests is the safe direction, so resolve literals with archy's own resolver, store them as a `string` edge kind read only by `affected` and `impact` (never `check`, `cycles`, `dsm`, `score` or `conventions`), turn it on by default for `affected` with an archy.yaml off switch, and mark tests selected only through a string edge.
- The other reads it as a scoping step only, per this issue's "data before code": a `bench/string_imports_scope.py` that reports new edges, non-redundant test edges, `affected` fan-out under the depth cap, and a hand-labelled sample of at least 100 non-redundant edges (mock.patch target, Django/Celery/settings path, logger name, other). Pre-register a build threshold (for example at least 80% precision on non-redundant test edges and a bounded median fan-out increase) and a decline threshold before labelling. Only on a pass, file an opt-in `string_imports:` feature restricted to `impact` and `affected`.

Both agree string edges must never enter `check`, `cycles` or the score. The open question this data does not settle is precision plus fan-out, which is what the pre-registered pass would measure.

Sources: https://www.pantsbuild.org/stable/reference/subsystems/python-infer , https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#analyze , https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/24058 .

Found by an adversarially-vetted research loop (two independent refuting reviewers per proposal).

- Does a constant-string `importlib.import_module("a.b.c")` become a real edge? That is resolvable and arguably a bug in the graph today rather than a blind spot to report.

## Done when

Either a written decision to close this as declined with the reason recorded, or a scoping pass that answers the distinguishing test above with data from real repositories - before any implementation.

**Prior art.** Two tools ship this as an opt-in heuristic. Pants `[python-infer]` has `string_imports` (default false), `string_imports_min_dots` (default 2), a `string_import_ignore` glob list and a `# pants: no-infer-dep` pragma. Ruff `[analyze]` has `detect-string-imports` (default false) and `string-imports-min-dots` (default 2), and ruff PR #24058 added a shorter-prefix fallback, so `"pkg.mod.fn"` resolves to `pkg.mod`. These are config docs, not precision data.

**Measured 2026-10-23.** `ruff analyze graph` with and without `--detect-string-imports` (ruff 0.15.12, min-dots 2) over the 40 `bench/cache/contract_clones` repos:
- 24 of 40 repos gain edges; 1,281 new edges in total.
- 938 of them come from test files.
- 593 test-sourced edges reach a module the test does not already reach statically. Those are tests `affected` misses today, spread over about 19 to 20 repos.
- Spot checks among those are true dependencies for test selection: `patch("thegent.agents.teammate_runner.TeammateRunner")`, `importlib.import_module("docvet.checks.freshness")` in a test, `monkeypatch.setattr("aai_cli.commands.llm.gateway.complete")`.
- Known false positives for architecture: logger names such as `LoggerAdapter("pkg.domain.abnormal")`.
- Fan-out risk: string edges into hub modules can make `affected` select nearly everything. 15M4C4R/ecosistemas-flujos-ia gains 85,848 (test, module) reachability pairs and AviralGup7/Singularity-Zero 17,869. The depth cap of 5 limits this only partly.
- The originally proposed example (mcp_coder) is not one: all 31 of its string edges are already reachable statically.

**How this bears on the distinguishing test.** The issue asks whether there is a repo where the signal is actionable rather than 0 or a wall of noise. For literal strings in tests, the answer looks like yes in about half the corpus. But the fan-out outliers show the noise case exists too.

**Where two independent reviewers split.**
- One reads it as a correctness fix to `affected`: over-selecting tests is the safe direction, so resolve literals with archy's own resolver, store them as a `string` edge kind read only by `affected` and `impact` (never `check`, `cycles`, `dsm`, `score` or `conventions`), turn it on by default for `affected` with an archy.yaml off switch, and mark tests selected only through a string edge.
- The other reads it as a scoping step only, per this issue's "data before code": a `bench/string_imports_scope.py` that reports new edges, non-redundant test edges, `affected` fan-out under the depth cap, and a hand-labelled sample of at least 100 non-redundant edges (mock.patch target, Django/Celery/settings path, logger name, other). Pre-register a build threshold (for example at least 80% precision on non-redundant test edges and a bounded median fan-out increase) and a decline threshold before labelling. Only on a pass, file an opt-in `string_imports:` feature restricted to `impact` and `affected`.

Both agree string edges must never enter `check`, `cycles` or the score. The open question this data does not settle is precision plus fan-out, which is what the pre-registered pass would measure.

Sources: https://www.pantsbuild.org/stable/reference/subsystems/python-infer , https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#analyze , https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/24058 .

fix(check): layers that name a third-party package give self-contradicting verdicts
open

**The gap.** A layer like `orm: {modules: ["sqlalchemy.**"]}` works by accident: external packages are graph nodes, so `forbid: [{from: domain, to: orm}]` does fire on `myapp.domain.model -> sqlalchemy`. Every other part of `check` treats the layer as nonexistent. Reproduced on f6fb600:

1. **Presence.** The same run that reports the violation also says "layers present: 1 of 2 declared; empty: orm". With `min_layers_present: 2` it adds "FAIL: 1 layer(s) present". `compute_coverage` skips external nodes before counting layer sizes (`src/archy/layers.py:373`).
2. **Coverage.** It prints "0 of 1 internal edges (0%)" next to the violation; with no violation, it claims "no forbid rule can fire", which is false.
3. **Contracts.** `archy contracts` and `check --contracts` return "no verdict ... Could not find package 'sqlalchemy'". `_archy_yaml_to_user_options` (`src/archy/contracts.py:330`) turns every pattern's first segment into a root package and never sets import-linter's `include_external_packages`.
4. **Sub-package patterns.** With `sqlalchemy.orm.**` and a real `from sqlalchemy.orm import Session`, `check` exits 0. External imports collapse to the top-level package (`src/archy/graph.py:556`), so the pattern can never match.

archy already treats external targets as legitimate for `required:` (`layers.py:639-640`), and the README's contracts example forbids `psycopg`. The `compute_coverage` docstring (`layers.py:364`) says the opposite.

**Anti-theater.** A false FAIL stops failing, an erroring command returns a verdict, and a rule that can never fire becomes an error. Each changes an exit code.

**Scope (one PR, each part on CLI text, CLI JSON and MCP, asserted on `model_dump()`).**
- (1) Layer sizes and presence count matched external nodes. A pattern matching no node at all is still empty.
- (2) Report internal-to-external governed edges as a separate count. Do not fold them into the internal edge ratio that #362/#355 protect; the fix is the false "nothing governed" claim, not the percentage.
- (3) Leave external roots (absent from the scanned tree, not guessed from pattern text) out of `root_packages`, and set `include_external_packages=True` when a forbidden layer names one. An external layer as the contract SOURCE raises a clear error.
- (4) An external pattern deeper than its top-level name raises `LayerConfigError` suggesting `sqlalchemy.**`. Decide it against the graph, not at YAML load, in both `check` and contracts.
- Fix the `layers.py:364` docstring; one README paragraph documenting external-package layers.

**Open design point.** One reviewer would accept either counting external edges or naming them separately; the other insists on a separate count. The separate count is the safer default.

**Acceptance.** Fixture: `myapp/domain/model.py` imports `sqlalchemy` and `sqlalchemy.orm`. Exit 1 with the violation, "layers present: 2 of 2", no presence FAIL, and `archy contracts` evaluates the contract. The `sqlalchemy.orm.**` form exits non-zero with the error. Mutation-verify each part separately (clear `__pycache__`).

**Out of scope.** A built-in third-party/stdlib selector (import-linter #278 parity): new capability with three reactions of demand. A top-level `rules:` key being silently ignored is covered by the strict-config-validation ticket.

**Sources.** import-linter `include_external_packages`: https://import-linter.readthedocs.io/en/stable/contract_types.html . import-linter #278: https://github.com/seddonym/import-linter/issues/278 . Internal vs external split in bsa-linter: https://github.com/defrag/bsa-python-linter .

Found by an adversarially-vetted research loop (two independent refuting reviewers per proposal).

hslee16: One more surface with the item 4 root cause (external imports collapse to the top-level package; on ee431ef that is `_external_target`, `src/archy/graph.py:1001`): `required:` rules.

A `must_reach` that names an external SUBMODULE can never match, because the graph only has the node `sqlalchemy`, never `sqlalchemy.orm`. The rule is then reported dead with exit 1, and the message gives a false reason: it says nothing imports the package any more, while the source imports it directly.

```bash
P=$(mktemp -d)/reqext && mkdir -p "$P/cmds" && cd "$P"
: > cmds/__init__.py
cat > cmds/setup.py <<'EOF'
from sqlalchemy.orm import registry
import sqlalchemy.orm
reg = registry()
EOF
cat > archy.yaml <<'EOF'
layers:
  cmds: {modules: ["cmds.**"]}
forbid: []
required:
  - {source: "cmds.setup", must_reach: "sqlalchemy.orm", reason: "mapper registry"}
EOF
archy check .; echo "exit=$?"
```

```
# 1 required-reach violation(s)

cmds.setup must reach sqlalchemy.orm:
  reason: mapper registry
  nothing matches the `must_reach` pattern 'sqlalchemy.orm' in the scanned tree: either the pattern is wrong, or -- for an external package -- no module imports it any more, which is itself the failure the rule is about.
exit=1
```

With `must_reach: sqlalchemy` the same file passes (exit 0). The first clause of the message ("the pattern is wrong") is arguably right; the second ("no module imports it any more") is false on its face, since `cmds/setup.py` line 1 imports it.

Scope note: the in-repo registry case in README:612 (`must_reach: app.core.database.model_registry`) works; only an external submodule target is affected.

Suggested addition to the item 4 scope: the same "external pattern deeper than its top-level name" check should cover `required.must_reach` (and `required.source`, for symmetry), raising `LayerConfigError` that suggests the top-level name, decided against the graph as item 4 already specifies. Until then, the dead-rule message (`src/archy/layers.py:686-692`) should not offer "no module imports it" when the pattern's first segment is an external node that IS imported.

Severity: low. Found by the 2026-11-04 codebase audit, verified by an independent reproduction, on `main` at ee431ef.

# An empty scope reports 0.0, not 1.0. "0 of 0 modules (100%)" is the exact
    # failure this class exists to prevent, reproduced inside it: a config whose
    # declared roots match nothing in the tree governs nothing, and saying it
    # governs everything is worse than saying nothing at all. Found by pointing
    # archy at a single-module project whose config named four layer packages.
    # `computed_field`, not a bare property: MCP tool returns are serialized with
    # `model_dump()`, which silently drops properties. Without this an agent
    # receiving `passed=false` for a presence shortfall got a coverage object
    # with nothing in it explaining why, which is the "indistinguishable from a
    # bug in archy" state this class exists to prevent, reproduced on the wire.
    @computed_field
    @property
    def module_ratio(self) -> float:
        return self.modules_matched / self.modules_total if self.modules_total else 0.0

    @computed_field
    @property
    def edge_ratio(self) -> float:
        return self.edges_governed / self.edges_total if self.edges_total else 0.0

    @computed_field
    @property
    def governs_no_edges(self) -> bool:
        """No import edge in the tree can be subject to any `forbid` rule.

        True both when internal edges exist and none has two layered endpoints,
        and when there are no internal edges at all. Either way every `forbid`
        rule is unfireable, so a clean verdict carries no information -- which
        is precisely what the verdict must say out loud.

        The threshold is exactly zero, not a percentage. Any other number is a
        policy choice about how much governance is "enough", which this module
        has no basis to pick; zero is the one value where "no violations found"
        is provably vacuous rather than merely thin.

        `computed_field`, not a property: `model_dump()` drops properties, and
        the MCP surface returns this object through `model_dump()`.
        """
        return self.edges_governed == 0

    @computed_field
    @property
    def governs_nothing(self) -> bool:
        """No module in the tree falls under any root the config names."""
        return self.modules_total == 0

    @computed_field
    @property
    def empty_layers(self) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        """Declared layers that matched no module at all."""
        return tuple(name for name, size in self.layer_sizes if size == 0)

    @computed_field
    @property
    def layers_present(self) -> int:
        return sum(1 for _, size in self.layer_sizes if size)


def governed_roots(config: LayerConfig) -> frozenset[str]:
    """The top-level packages the config's LAYER PATTERNS talk about.

    A pattern is a dotted-name glob whose first segment names the namespace the
    author intended to govern, except a floating one (`**.services.**`), which
    names no namespace. Any floating pattern makes the scope unbounded, so this
    returns the empty set and `compute_coverage` does not scope by root.

    NOT `LayerConfig.roots`, despite the name proximity. That field declares
    extra PEP 420 scan roots so the graph builder can find namespace packages at
    all; this function asks which namespaces the rules claim authority over.
    Neither reads the other.
    """
    patterns = [pattern for layer in config.layers for pattern in layer.patterns]
    if any(is_floating_pattern(pattern) for pattern in patterns):
        return frozenset()
    return frozenset(pattern.split(".")[0] for pattern in patterns)

    """Translate archy layer patterns into import-linter module expressions.

    The two dialects disagree on one thing, and it is the one archy tells
    people to write. archy's `pkg.**` means "pkg AND every descendant"
    (`layers._translate_pattern` collapses the dot so the bare parent
    matches); import-linter's `pkg.**` means the descendants ONLY. So
    `shipping.store.**` on a leaf module resolved to the empty set, the
    Forbidden contract had no source modules, and a project with a real
    forbidden transitive path reported a clean pass at exit 0 (#435).

    Dropping the trailing `.**` restores archy's meaning exactly, because
    import-linter's `as_packages` (on by default) already reads a named
    package as itself plus its descendants. Emitting the wildcard as well
    would add nothing and would report `pkg.**` as matching no module every
    time `pkg` is a leaf, which is noise archy itself generated.

    Nothing else is rewritten. A bare `pkg` keeps whatever `as_packages`
    gives it, which is how every existing config already behaves.
    """
    expressions: list[str] = []
    for pattern in patterns:
        expressions.append(pattern[: -len(".**")] if pattern.endswith(".**") else pattern)
    return list(dict.fromkeys(expressions))

def run_check(path: Path, *, config_path: Path | None) -> CheckPayload | CheckErrorPayload:
    if config_path is None:
        discovered = discover_config(path)
        if discovered is None:
            # Tier-3 recoverable precondition: no config to check against. In-band
            # (isError:false) so the agent can branch and create/point at a config,
            # not a raise. A *malformed* config below still raises (tier 2).
            return CheckErrorPayload(
                error=f"no archy.yaml found near {path}; pass config_path or create one."
            )
        config_path = discovered
    config = load_config(config_path)
    graph = _build_graph(path, **scan_kwargs(config))
    violations = find_violations(graph, config)
    reach_violations = find_reach_violations(graph, config)
    sdp_violations: list[SdpViolation] = []
    if config.sdp.enabled:
        sdp_violations = find_sdp_violations(graph, tolerance=config.sdp.tolerance)
    sdp_fails_gate = bool(sdp_violations) and config.sdp.mode == "error"
    coverage = compute_coverage(graph, config)
    # The presence floor gates `passed` here exactly as it gates the CLI's exit
    # code. Wiring it into one surface and not the other was the first cut, and
    # it left the AGENT-FACING surface reporting passed=true on the degenerate
    # single-module solution the check exists to catch: the case an agent in a
    # course-correction loop most needs to be told about.
    presence_fails = (
        config.min_layers_present is not None
        and coverage.layers_present < config.min_layers_present
    )
    unverified = contracts_unverified(config, coverage, violations)
    return CheckPayload(
        config_path=str(config_path),
        violations=tuple(violations),
        sdp_violations=tuple(sdp_violations),
        required_violations=tuple(reach_violations),
        passed=(
            not violations and not reach_violations and not sdp_fails_gate and not presence_fails
        ),
        coverage=coverage,
        presence_fails=presence_fails,
        min_layers_present=config.min_layers_present,
        transitive_checked=False,
        transitive_unverified_reason=(
            (
                f"{len(config.forbid)} forbid "
                f"{'rule' if len(config.forbid) == 1 else 'rules'} declared, but this check "
                "governs too little of the graph to verify them; it sees DIRECT edges only. "
                "Call archy_check(contracts=True) to evaluate them transitively via "
                "import-linter, which sees paths a direct-edge check cannot."
            )
            if unverified
            else None

    """Return the layer name covering `qualname`, or None if unlayered.

    Layers are expected to be disjoint. That is checked here at runtime (the
    walk collects all matches and raises if a module matches more than one),
    not at load_config, which validates pattern *syntax* but not cross-layer
    overlap. Disjointness can only be decided against a concrete module set.
    """
    matches = [layer.name for layer in layers if _qualname_matches_any(qualname, layer.patterns)]
    if len(matches) > 1:
        raise LayerConfigError(
            f"module {qualname!r} matches multiple layers ({', '.join(matches)}); "
            "make pattern coverage disjoint"

    return matches[0] if matches else None

    for source, target, data in graph.edges(data=True):

        tgt_layer = match_layer(target, config.layers)

"""Wrap import-linter's contract checks behind a stable archy interface.

archy.yaml ships direct-edge layer rules; import-linter ships transitive
contracts (Layers, Forbidden, Independence, Protected, AcyclicSiblings).
This module surfaces import-linter results as frozen pydantic models, ready
for `archy contracts` (CLI) or `archy_check(contracts=True)` (MCP, which
nests the result under `CheckPayload.contracts`) to consume.

Config resolution order:
  1. Explicit `config_filename` argument (.importlinter or pyproject.toml).
  2. `.importlinter` in the project root: the canonical contracts config.
     Supports all five contract types (Layers, Forbidden, Independence,
     Protected, AcyclicSiblings) and `ignore_imports` whitelists for
     legitimate transitive edges. Recommended for any project that needs
     more than a clean direct-edge rule.
  3. `archy.yaml` in the project root, translated to a list of Forbidden
     contracts (one per `forbid` rule). Best-effort fallback so a project
     with only an archy.yaml can run `archy contracts` without extra
     config; emits a UserWarning because this path cannot express
     `ignore_imports` (transitive false-positives are unavoidable).

def _make_external_target_project(tmp_path: Path, *, bootstrap: str) -> Path:
    """A `required:` rule whose `must_reach` is an EXTERNAL package."""
    app = tmp_path / "app"
    (app / "commands").mkdir(parents=True)
    (app / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (app / "commands" / "__init__.py").write_text(bootstrap)
    (app / "commands" / "setup_user.py").write_text("x = 1\n")
    (tmp_path / "archy.yaml").write_text(
        "layers: {}\nforbid: []\n"
        "required:\n  - source: 'app.commands.*'\n    must_reach: sqlalchemy\n"
    )
    return tmp_path


def test_snapshot_agrees_with_check_on_an_external_target(tmp_path: Path):
    """`check` and `snapshot` must not disagree about the same tree.

    They did: `check` keeps external nodes, but the snapshot path stripped them
    before the reach check ran, so `must_reach: sqlalchemy` reported as a dead
    rule ("cannot fire") while `check` reported it satisfied.
    """
    project = _make_external_target_project(tmp_path, bootstrap="import sqlalchemy\n")

    assert CliRunner().invoke(main, ["check", str(project)]).exit_code == 0
    assert CliRunner().invoke(main, ["snapshot", str(project)]).exit_code == 0

    baseline = json.loads((project / ".archy" / "baseline.json").read_text())
    assert baseline["required_violations"] == []


def test_diff_catches_a_removed_external_bootstrap_import(tmp_path: Path):
    """The masking this caused was worse than the wrong verdict.

    A false "dead rule" landed on BOTH sides of the diff, so deleting the
    bootstrap import could never surface as a regression -- the exact ratchet
    the feature exists to provide, silently disabled for external targets.
    """
    project = _make_external_target_project(tmp_path, bootstrap="import sqlalchemy\n")
    assert CliRunner().invoke(main, ["snapshot", str(project)]).exit_code == 0

    (project / "app" / "commands" / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    result = CliRunner().invoke(main, ["diff", str(project)])

    assert "required-reach: +1 added" in result.output
    # For an external target, "nothing matches it" IS the failure: the import
    pkg.mkdir()
    (pkg / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (pkg / "a.py").write_text("from pkg.b import thing\n")
    (pkg / "b.py").write_text("")
    (pkg / "c.py").write_text("from pkg.a import other\n")
    return tmp_path


def test_check_passed_respects_the_layer_presence_floor(tmp_path: Path):
    """The gate has to hold on the AGENT-FACING surface, not just the CLI.

    It shipped wired into `archy check` only, so `archy_check` reported
    passed=True for the degenerate single-module solution the floor exists to
    catch: precisely the case an agent in a correction loop needs told.
    """

    (tmp_path / "app").mkdir()
    (tmp_path / "app" / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (tmp_path / "app" / "everything.py").write_text("x = 1\n")
    (tmp_path / "archy.yaml").write_text(
        "min_layers_present: 2\n"
        "layers:\n"
        "  routes:\n    modules: ['app.routes.**']\n"
        "  services:\n    modules: ['app.services.**']\n"
        "forbid:\n  - {from: services, to: routes}\n"
    )

    payload = run_check(tmp_path, config_path=None)

    assert isinstance(payload, CheckPayload)
    assert payload.violations == ()
    assert payload.passed is False

    # Asserted on the SERIALIZED form, not attributes. FastMCP sends
    # `model_dump()`, which drops plain properties, so an attribute-only
    # assertion passed while the agent-facing payload carried no reason at all.
    dumped = payload.model_dump()
    assert dumped["passed"] is False
    assert dumped["presence_fails"] is True
    assert dumped["min_layers_present"] == 2
    assert dumped["coverage"]["layers_present"] == 0
    assert sorted(dumped["coverage"]["empty_layers"]) == ["routes", "services"]


def test_create_server_registers_expected_tools():
    server = create_server()
    assert not result.all_kept
    assert result.broken == 1


def _write_transitive_fixture(root: Path, *, patterns: str) -> None:
    """top.store -> top.service -> top.api, with store forbidden from api.

    The violation is reachable ONLY transitively: there is no direct
    store -> api edge, which is the entire reason `contracts` exists next to
    `check`. `patterns` selects the dialect the layers are written in.
    """
    pkg = root / "top"
    pkg.mkdir()
    (pkg / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (pkg / "api.py").write_text("VALUE = 1\n")
    (pkg / "service.py").write_text("from top import api  # noqa: F401\n")
    (pkg / "store.py").write_text("from top import service  # noqa: F401\n")
    (root / "archy.yaml").write_text(
        textwrap.dedent(
            f"""
            layers:
              api:
                modules:
                  - "top.api{patterns}"
              service:
                modules:
                  - "top.service{patterns}"
              store:
                modules:
                  - "top.store{patterns}"
            forbid:
              - {{from: store, to: api}}
            """
        ).strip()
        + "\n"
    )

"""Layers that name a third-party package (#527).

`orm: {modules: ["thirdpartyorm.**"]}` always fired on a direct import, because
external packages are graph nodes, while presence, coverage and contracts all
treated the layer as nonexistent. Each part is asserted on every surface that
reports it, on the serialized form (`model_dump()`), because FastMCP sends that
and drops plain properties.

`thirdpartyorm` is not installed anywhere: an external package only has to be
imported by the scanned tree to become a node.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
from pathlib import Path

import pytest
from click.testing import CliRunner

from archy.cli import main
from archy.contracts import ContractsConfigError, run_contracts
from archy.graph import build_graph
from archy.layers import LayerConfigError, compute_coverage, find_violations, load_config
from archy.mcp_runs import run_check
from archy.mcp_payloads import CheckPayload

EXTERNAL = "thirdpartyorm"


def _project(
    root: Path,
    *,
    domain_imports_orm: bool,
    orm_pattern: str = f"{EXTERNAL}.**",
    extra_yaml: str = "",
) -> Path:
    """`myapp.domain.model` and `myapp.service.repo`; only `repo` always imports the ORM."""
    for package in ("myapp", "myapp/domain", "myapp/service"):
        (root / package).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        (root / package / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    domain = f"import {EXTERNAL}\nfrom {EXTERNAL}.orm import Session\n"
    (root / "myapp/domain/model.py").write_text(domain if domain_imports_orm else "x = 1\n")
    (root / "myapp/service/repo.py").write_text(f"import {EXTERNAL}\n")
    (root / "archy.yaml").write_text(
        "layers:\n"
        "  domain: {modules: ['myapp.domain.**']}\n"
        "  service: {modules: ['myapp.service.**']}\n"
        f"  orm: {{modules: ['{orm_pattern}']}}\n"
        "forbid:\n  - {from: domain, to: orm}\n" + extra_yaml
    )
    return root


def test_a_layer_naming_an_external_package_is_present(tmp_path: Path):
    root = _project(tmp_path, domain_imports_orm=True)
    config = load_config(root / "archy.yaml")
    graph = build_graph(root)

    coverage = compute_coverage(graph, config)

    # The fixture reaches the branch: the layer's only member is an external node.
    assert [n for n, d in graph.nodes(data=True) if d.get("external")] == [EXTERNAL]
    assert dict(coverage.layer_sizes)["orm"] == 1
    assert coverage.empty_layers == ()
    assert coverage.layers_present == 3
    # Two edges reach the ORM (domain.model, service.repo); both are layered.
    assert coverage.external_edges_governed == 2
    # The internal ratio is untouched: no internal edge exists in this tree.
    assert (coverage.edges_total, coverage.edges_governed) == (0, 0)
    assert coverage.governs_no_edges is False
    assert [v.target for v in find_violations(graph, config)] == [EXTERNAL]


def test_a_pattern_matching_no_node_at_all_is_still_an_empty_layer(tmp_path: Path):
    root = _project(tmp_path, domain_imports_orm=True, orm_pattern="neverimported.**")
    coverage = compute_coverage(build_graph(root), load_config(root / "archy.yaml"))

    assert coverage.empty_layers == ("orm",)
    assert coverage.external_edges_governed == 0

`archy check --contracts` runs this same transitive verdict inline, nested under the check output. It never changes `check`'s own exit code: a flag that can turn a passing check into a failing one because an optional dependency is absent would be unsafe to leave on in CI. Use the standalone `archy contracts` when the transitive result should itself gate the build.

**A kept contract is not automatically protection.** A contract whose module expressions match nothing in the graph holds no matter what the code does, so `all_kept` calls it kept while nothing was ever checked. `archy contracts` exits non-zero on `verified` (evaluated *and* held), not on `all_kept`, and `archy check --contracts` reports `transitive_checked: false` for the same reason: a rule that could not have failed was not evaluated. The text output marks such a contract `??` rather than `OK` and names the expressions that matched no module; `--format json` adds top-level `verified` and `unverifiable` alongside `kept`/`broken`, and per-contract `matched_nothing` and `unmatched_expressions`. A `.importlinter` `type = layers` contract needs no such flag: import-linter itself refuses to run when a required layer's module is absent, which archy reports as a config error, and an optional layer (written `(name)`) is absent by design.

**Config resolution.** `archy contracts` reads, in order:

1. The `--config` argument if passed.
2. `.importlinter` in the project root: the **canonical** contracts config.
3. `archy.yaml`: best-effort fallback. Each `forbid:` rule becomes one Forbidden contract checked transitively. Emits a `UserWarning` because this path cannot express `ignore_imports`, so any legitimate transitive edge (e.g., a service layer reaching `psycopg` *through* a sanctioned `app.libs.db.*` module) will be reported as a violation with no way to whitelist it.

### Enforce layer rules

Reads `archy.yaml` from the repo root. Exits 1 on any violation. See [Layer rules](#layer-rules-archy-check) below.

```bash
archy check path/to/project
archy check path/to/project --format json

```

### Transitive contracts (`archy contracts`)

`archy check` only sees direct edges. `archy contracts` wraps [import-linter](https://import-linter.readthedocs.io/) so the same layer story is enforced *transitively* (A → B → C still counts as A reaching C). It is the strictness upgrade for projects whose layers leak through indirect paths.

A layer that names a third-party package (`orm: {modules: ["sqlalchemy.**"]}`) fired on a direct import but was treated as nonexistent everywhere else in `check`. Each part below is on CLI text, CLI JSON and the MCP payload.

**1. Presence.** External nodes a layer matches now count toward `layer_sizes`, so `layers present` is right and `min_layers_present` no longer fails on a layer that exists. A pattern matching no node at all is still an empty layer.

**2. Coverage.** Edges from a layered internal module into a layered external package are a separate count, `external_edges_governed` (text: "N internal-to-external edge(s) governed"). content.text:
PR #832 is open at https://github.com/hslee16/Archy/pull/832 and closes #527. It fixes all four parts of the ticket, plus the `required:` message from the audit comment. I haven't run a DeepWork review round on it yet, and I haven't merged it. The full suite and ruff, ty and the `archy` gates pass.

**The four parts**
- **Presence:** external nodes that a layer matches now count toward `layers present`, so `min_layers_present` no longer fails on a layer that exists. A pattern that matches no node is still reported as empty.
- **Coverage:** edges into a layered external package are reported separately as `external_edges_governed`. They are not mixed into the internal edge ratio. A clean run also stops claiming "no forbid rule can fire" when one can.
- **Contracts:** `archy contracts` and `check --contracts` now evaluate these rules instead of returning "Could not find package". An external layer as the source of a forbid rule gets a clear error.
- **Sub-package patterns:** a pattern like `sqlalchemy.orm.**` is refused with a suggestion to use `sqlalchemy.**`. This applies in `check`, the MCP check and contracts, and to `required:` `source`, `must_reach` and `within`. The false "no module imports it" reason is gone.

I also fixed the stale `compute_coverage` docstring and added a README paragraph.

**Gotchas**
- **String option:** import-linter only accepts `include_external_packages` as the string `"True"`. A real boolean is read as false.
- **`contracts.py` scan:** it now builds the graph to find the scanned tree's roots. It applies `exclude:` and `roots:` but not the `max_modules` guard, because import-linter walks the tree itself. That is a small behaviour change worth a look.

**Tests:** `tests/test_external_layers.py` has 17 tests across CLI text, CLI JSON, the MCP payload and contracts. I broke the code 11 ways, one per part, and every break failed a test.

Do you want me to run the DeepWork review on #832 before you look at it?

lastPrompt: is archy being used within the deepwork review?

content.text:
Yes, in one of the reviewers. The local `.deepreview` file defines `archy_grounded_structural_review`, which tells the reviewer to run archy's own CLI from the repo root rather than reason by hand.

**What it runs**
- **`archy impact`:** transitive importers of each changed file.
- **`archy affected`:** depth-capped list of affected tests.
- **`archy cycles`:** new import cycles involving changed modules.
- **`archy check`:** layer-rule violations.
- **`archy what-to-refactor-next`:** only to see whether a changed module is a top edit-risk candidate.

It must put the archy command and output next to each finding. On #828 its report cited exactly these commands, for example 22 transitive dependents and 15 affected tests. For #832 it hasn't finished yet.

The reviewer has Bash but no archy MCP server, so it uses the CLI via `uv run archy`, not the `mcp__archy__` tools.

**What doesn't use archy.** The other reviewers read the diff and apply rules: em-dashes, docs drift, Python conventions, docstring accuracy and "suggest new reviews". They don't call archy.

The `.deepreview` file is gitignored on purpose, so this setup exists only on this machine and isn't part of the repo.

fix(contracts): a forbidden path through a subdirectory without __init__.py reports a clean pass
open

**The gap.** grimp, the engine under `archy contracts` and `check --contracts`, deliberately prunes any directory without `__init__.py` once it is inside a regular package (grimp 3.14, `adaptors/modulefinder.py`: "we won't include 'orphans'"). Nothing reports it, so a transitive path through such a directory is invisible.

**Repro.** `pkg/a.py` imports `pkg.ns.mid`; `pkg/ns/mid.py` (no `pkg/ns/__init__.py`) imports `pkg.b`; a forbidden contract says `pkg.a` must not reach `pkg.b`. `archy contracts` prints "1 kept, 0 broken (3 modules, 0 imports)" and exits 0. Add `pkg/ns/__init__.py` and it reports "1 broken via pkg.a -> pkg.ns.mid -> pkg.b".

On a real repo: `grimp.build_graph('flask')` on `bench/repo_cache/flask/src` has 21 modules and zero `flask.sansio.*`, because `src/flask/sansio/` has no `__init__.py`. Of archy's 110 internal flask edges, 26 touch sansio. A rough scan found namespace subdirectories under a regular package in 6 of 35 cached repos (some may be data or vendored dirs).

This is the same "clean pass that is not" class as #435, #456, #457 and #458. The existing `unverifiable`/`verified` fields on `ContractsResult` (`src/archy/contracts.py:78-109`) do not catch it, and `_expression_coverage` only flags contract expressions that match no module.

**Anti-theater.** The user stops trusting a pass that was never computed, and either adds the `__init__.py` or knows those modules are only covered by direct-edge `check`.

**Fix (both reviewers).** Mirror grimp's own pruning rule with a filesystem walk: under each configured root package's directory, list subdirectories that contain `.py` files but no `__init__.py`. Do **not** diff against archy's graph: standalone `archy contracts` never builds it, and tests, examples, src layouts and `roots:` produce spurious mismatches.

Expose the list on `ContractsResult` (for example `unscanned_dirs: tuple[str, ...]`) and render "N modules not visible to the contracts engine (subdirectory without `__init__.py`): ..." on all three surfaces in one change: `_contracts_to_text` / `_contracts_to_dict` (`src/archy/cli.py:2747-2787`), the `check --contracts` text and JSON next to the transitive note, and the MCP `archy_check` contracts payload, asserted on `model_dump()`.

**Open design point.** One reviewer makes `verified` a `@computed_field` that turns false when `unscanned_dirs` is non-empty (the #435/#457 precedent). The other only qualifies the verdict with the note. Changing `verified` alters exit behaviour for existing users, so decide it explicitly.

**Acceptance.** The fixture above. First assert `pkg/ns/__init__.py` does not exist and grimp's graph lacks `pkg.ns.mid`; then assert the note on CLI JSON and `model_dump()`. Mutation check: remove the scan, clear `__pycache__`, confirm red.

**Out of scope.** A cross-engine differential bench (`bench/engine_differential.py`) and the re-export disagreement class, which is #436. File the bench separately if wanted.

**Sources.** grimp: https://github.com/python-grimp/grimp . Same gap reported upstream as import-linter #96 (PEP 420 subpackages unsupported): https://github.com/seddonym/import-linter/issues/96 .

Found by an adversarially-vetted research loop (two independent refuting reviewers per proposal).
